method.setting: Each zero-shot model was told which failure to look for and was tested on samples that have that failure or none. Its score is a single-prompt, mode-primed estimate, not a product.
method.metric: J = TPR - FPR, on the answers that carry a verdict. 0% is chance, 100% flags every bad sample and no clean one. J is the sort key within a mode; each row also has false alarms per 100 clean changes and precision at 1%, 5% and 20% prevalence.
method.unreadable: An answer with no verdict (failed call, blocked request, text cut by the token budget, no verdict in the text) is unreadable: it is left out of the rates and counted beside them, per label. j_strict is J under the old rule that counted such answers as 'not flagged'; j_bounds is J if every unreadable answer had been wrong, and right.
method.intervals: 95% intervals. TPR and FPR: Wilson. J: Newcombe where samples are independent; where samples are grouped (task, pair, API pair, file) whole groups are resampled (100,000 draws, fixed seed).
method.paired: Two rows are compared on the samples both have a readable verdict for; the difference of their J gets a 95% bootstrap interval (groups resampled where the mode has them). 'Ahead', 'worse' and a single winner need an interval that excludes 0 at the published precision: a bound that prints as 0.0% does not exclude 0.
method.best: Best reviewer: the best ranked row of a mode that is not marked incomplete. A row with under 95% readable answers in one class is listed and ranked, with its J bounds, but is never named best reviewer or sole winner; if its J is higher than the best reviewer's it stays in the top group. Not ranked: baseline rules, shortcut baselines and rows outside a tool's design scope. Top group: the best reviewer and every ranked row whose paired difference from it includes 0. Best catalog tool: the best tool of the SAICA catalog that ran its own check; a framework that ran our rule text is not a candidate.
method.tiers: Tiers describe the best reviewer's J on our set, not how well a failure is caught in use: J 80% or more on our set; J 25% to under 80% on our set; J under 25% on our set.
method.cost: A row's cost covers every call made to get its scored answers: the current answer of each sample plus earlier attempts that failed or were cut off and had to be re-run. Smoke tests, runs on earlier versions of a set and accidental duplicate answers are not included. Cost per 1,000 reviews is that cost divided by the reviews made, for one mode-specific question per review.

A rule with no knowledge of any library (does the name appear anywhere else in the file?) scores J +60%. It catches 98% of the undefined names, 99% of the fake methods and 35% of the fake imports: the fakes are one-token changes spliced into human code.

144 of the 348 fakes fail in Delulu's own check with a plain 'name is not defined': a scope error, not a made-up library API. Fake imports are the part that needs library knowledge; there the models catch 66% to 94%.

15 scored rows are noisy (a 'fake' import that did not fail, clean originals that are broken files) and the 348 fakes hold 308 distinct completions. Leaving both out changes a J by -1.3 to +4.2 points, while the four highest-scoring models are only 1.3 points apart.

Both kinds pass the task's functional tests; vulnerable ones fail the hidden CVE security test. The labels come from two versions of the SusVibes security tests: 17 runs (1,187 patches) were judged by v1.0 and 9 runs (515 patches) by the older v0.0, which upstream replaced. 5 of the 26 runs were given security hints; 2 of those were shown the hidden security test. Identical patches kept once; patches over 60k characters left out.

AI tools see the task text and the agent's diff. bandit and semgrep run on the patched files and flag a patch when a finding lands on a line it added. bandit has two rows: its default profile, and with the assert rule (B101) skipped and test files left out. giskard and promptfoo wrap the same review in their own judge template, with deepseek-v4-flash as the judge.
Same review prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-19/20.

Also tried on a 417-patch held-out subset (projects kept apart): claude-opus-4-8 at low effort J -3%, Kimi-K2.6 J +4%, Muse Glimmer 30B before fine-tuning J -11%, Muse Glimmer 30B after fine-tuning on 682 patches (341 vulnerable, 341 secure) drawn from the 1,285 patches of the other projects J -2%.

The three Claude models (run 2026-11-22) were called through Claude Code in headless mode on a subscription, not through an API: one process per sample with every tool switched off and an empty working folder, the same prompt as the other models plus a one-line system prompt and Claude Code's environment note, default sampling (Claude Code has no temperature setting) and thinking on (it cannot be switched off for these models). No effort level was set: the calls ran at Claude Code's default, which is medium for each of these models (checked 2026-11-22 with the same flags and the same Claude Code version).
caveats: Each zero-shot model was told which failure to look for and was tested on samples that have that failure or none. Its score is a single-prompt, mode-primed estimate, not a product.

Answers with no verdict are left out of the rates; they are not counted as 'not flagged'. Unreadable: ultramarine-1-flash 233 of 1,702 (165 bad, 68 clean; mostly answers cut by the token budget); deepseek-v4.1-flash 160 of 1,702 (90 bad, 70 clean; mostly answers cut by the token budget); PR-Agent 157 of 1,702 (88 bad, 69 clean; mostly the tool failed to run); semgrep 51 of 1,702 (32 bad, 19 clean; mostly the sample could not be prepared for the tool); bandit 51 of 1,702 (32 bad, 19 clean; mostly the sample could not be prepared for the tool); bandit (no assert check) 51 of 1,702 (32 bad, 19 clean; mostly the sample could not be prepared for the tool); deepseek-v4-flash 42 of 1,702 (18 bad, 24 clean; mostly requests the provider blocked); minimax-m3 28 of 1,702 (7 bad, 21 clean; mostly requests the provider blocked); mimo-v2.6-flash 25 of 1,702 (5 bad, 20 clean; mostly requests the provider blocked); promptfoo 25 of 1,702 (5 bad, 20 clean; mostly requests the provider blocked); giskard 23 of 1,702 (6 bad, 17 clean; mostly the tool failed to run); gpt-oss-20b (self-hosted) 22 of 1,702 (10 bad, 12 clean; mostly answers cut by the token budget); Qwen3.8-27B (self-hosted) 1 of 1,702 (1 bad, 0 clean; mostly requests the provider blocked). Marked incomplete (under 95% readable in one class): ultramarine-1-flash, deepseek-v4.1-flash, PR-Agent, deepseek-v4-flash.

On SusVibes no reviewer separates vulnerable from secure patches from the diff alone: the highest J is +23% (95% interval +12% to +34% when tasks are resampled), and 0 of the other 18 rows have a J inside that interval. No best reviewer can be named.

The label is mostly decided by the task, not by the patch: in 42 of 166 tasks every patch is vulnerable and in 20 every patch is secure. A rule that never reads the patch (are the other agents' patches for this task mostly vulnerable?) scores J +49%; 'shorter than the median patch' scores +17%.

Within tasks that have both labels the AI models score J +3% to +29% (over all patches: -3% to +23%). What signal there is concerns which patch of a task is the vulnerable one, not which tasks are dangerous.

The labels come from two versions of the security tests: 515 of 1702 patches (38% of the secure ones) were judged by SusVibes v0.0 tests, which upstream replaced in v1.0 because they can reject secure code. 5 of 26 agent runs were given security hints; 2 of them were shown the hidden security test and wrote 23% of the secure patches.

On the clean subset (v1.0 labels, no test-exposed run: 904 vulnerable, 283 secure) every J is between -6% and +21%. Leaving out the 16 tasks whose security test checks the text of an error message changes a J by -1 to +5 points.
bandit's J of -8% came from assert findings (rule B101) in test files that agents added. With B101 skipped and test files left out it is +1%: no signal either way.

Only 45 of 166 tasks have a weakness class that bandit and semgrep rule packs target; the others are logic-level (information exposure, resource limits, authorisation). On those 45 tasks semgrep scores J +2% and bandit (B101 skipped) +1%.

Check of the setup: each model was shown, one diff at a time, the reference code with the CVE fix and the same code with the fix reverted (182 pairs). The 3 models tried reach J +10% to +15%, so the low scores are not a scoring bug. The two versions were never shown side by side. Opus at medium effort, on 50 of the pairs, flags the vulnerable version and not the fixed one in 6.

Label check: one model (Opus, medium effort), shown the CWE, the CVE fix and the security test, agreed with 31 of 40 'vulnerable' labels and 8 of 10 'secure' ones (95% interval for the secure ones: 49% to 94%). An independent relabel of 210 patches has 17 done. No noise correction is applied to any J.
A 'secure' label means the patch passes the test for one CVE; other weaknesses are not ruled out.

Every label re-checked by running the code against its tests (the original asserts of MBPP and HumanEval; MBPP has three per task): crashes, timeouts, 'wrong' outputs that actually pass and reference solutions that fail were dropped.
Reviewers see the task description and the function, not the tests. Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-20.

The three Claude models (run 2026-11-22) were called through Claude Code in headless mode on a subscription, not through an API: one process per sample with every tool switched off and an empty working folder, the same prompt as the other models plus a one-line system prompt and Claude Code's environment note, default sampling (Claude Code has no temperature setting) and thinking on (it cannot be switched off for these models). No effort level was set: the calls ran at Claude Code's default, which is medium for each of these models (checked 2026-11-22 with the same flags and the same Claude Code version).
caveats: Short, self-contained functions from two famous public problem sets: models may know the right answers, so expect lower scores on real agent code.
Type checkers and linters look for a different kind of bug; they are here as a floor, not as fair competitors.

KG tools run through their own built-in check, with deepseek-v4-flash as their model: uqlm re-solves the task 5 times and flags code that disagrees with most re-solves; it was run on the first 300 + 300 functions only (it makes 10 model calls per review).
Each zero-shot model was told which failure to look for and was tested on samples that have that failure or none. Its score is a single-prompt, mode-primed estimate, not a product.

Answers with no verdict are left out of the rates; they are not counted as 'not flagged'. Unreadable: Phi-4-mini 117 of 2,440 (69 bad, 48 clean; mostly answers without a verdict); uqlm 23 of 600 (1 bad, 22 clean; mostly no score returned); deepseek-v4-flash 8 of 2,440 (0 bad, 8 clean; mostly answers cut by the token budget); mimo-v2.6-flash 4 of 2,440 (1 bad, 3 clean; mostly answers cut by the token budget); PR-Agent 1 of 2,440 (0 bad, 1 clean; mostly the tool failed to run). Marked incomplete (under 95% readable in one class): Phi-4-mini, uqlm.
Run on part of the samples: uqlm (300 bad + 300 clean). Their rates are on those samples, and comparisons with other rows use only the samples both ran on.
The headline J blends two problem sets. For the three highest-scoring models, J is +94% to +96% on HumanEval and +72% to +82% on MBPP.

65% of the wrong functions were written by open code models of 8 billion parameters or fewer (2023-24). On the 98 wrong functions of the one recent generator, gpt-4o-mini, the same three models catch 69% to 86% (other generators: 88% to 100%), and their J against the reference solutions of the same tasks is +58% to +77%. The surface classifier (code tokens only) scores +30% on those rows.

Every correct function is a reference solution and every wrong one is model-written, so layout gives the label away: a classifier that sees only code tokens, never the task, scores J +39%, and four formatting cues score +35%.

Labels follow the hidden asserts, while reviewers are told to judge against the task text only. On MBPP, 52 of 882 'wrong' functions are flagged by none of the three highest-scoring models and 35 of 477 'correct' ones by all three; a hand check of 24 of these rows in the review of 21 November 2026 found the label did not hold under that question in 19.
Textbook functions written by pre-agent models: this mode should not be averaged with the modes that score agent patches.

Each zero-shot model was told which failure to look for and was tested on samples that have that failure or none. Its score is a single-prompt, mode-primed estimate, not a product.

Run on part of the samples: Opik (150 bad + 150 clean); PR-Agent (150 bad + 150 clean). Their rates are on those samples, and comparisons with other rows use only the samples both ran on.

What is measured: the agent declared the task done and the issue's hidden tests fail. That covers wrong fixes as well as unfinished work, so the result is about false 'done' claims, not about the knowledge graph's incomplete execution (skipped or stubbed subtasks).

The label is mostly decided by the issue, not by the run: 64% of the failing runs come from issues the agent solves in none of its other runs, and 64% of the passing runs from issues it solves in all of them. A rule that never sees the run (do the agent's other runs of this issue mostly fail?) scores J +61%; the highest reviewer J is +46%.

On issues with both outcomes (208 failing, 214 passing runs) the three highest-scoring models reach J +9% to +38%, each with an interval of about +/-9 points; on the pure issues they reach +27% to +50%.
The closing message carries no signal: it says the tests pass in 75% of the failing runs and 78% of the passing ones.
The issues and their hidden tests are mined automatically (SWE-rebench) and were not checked by people, so some failing runs may fail because the tests ask for more than the issue text says.

setup: 175 correct agent patches (Qwen3-Coder-480B in OpenHands, hidden tests pass) with ONE unrequested change injected by claude-opus-4-8, vs 175 correct patches from other issues left as they are.

Injected changes, 2-15 lines, in five kinds: drive-by refactor, cleanup, extra feature, quiet behaviour change, added logging/config. 127 sit in a file the agent already edited, 48 in another file of the same package. Each was checked to still parse; a sample was checked by hand.

Both sides use only near-minimal patches (no bigger than the reference fix allows) and are matched exactly on how many source files they change (23 injected patches without an exact match were dropped), so the file count does not give the label away. Size is not matched: a count of hunks scores J +47% (shortcut rows).

Reviewers see the issue and the patch. Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-21 on version 1.1 of the set, in which one diff generator writes every patch of both classes; the first run (2026-11-20, version 1.0) is kept as a stratum. Building the set cost $13 of Opus calls, failed attempts included (not part of any tool's cost).

The three Claude models (run 2026-11-22) were called through Claude Code in headless mode on a subscription, not through an API: one process per sample with every tool switched off and an empty working folder, the same prompt as the other models plus a one-line system prompt and Claude Code's environment note, default sampling (Claude Code has no temperature setting) and thinking on (it cannot be switched off for these models). No effort level was set: the calls ran at Claude Code's default, which is medium for each of these models (checked 2026-11-22 with the same flags and the same Claude Code version).
caveats: Synthetic: the unrequested changes were written by a model on purpose. Natural scope creep may be subtler or messier.
All patches come from one agent (Qwen3-Coder-480B with OpenHands).

None of the KG's scope-creep tools has a built-in check for a finished patch: 20 of 22 prevent it during the run (approval gates, allow-lists, sandboxes); the other 2 (promptfoo, DeepEval) are general LLM judges that would only run a rubric we wrote, which the zero-shot models already measure.
Each zero-shot model was told which failure to look for and was tested on samples that have that failure or none. Its score is a single-prompt, mode-primed estimate, not a product.

Answers with no verdict are left out of the rates; they are not counted as 'not flagged'. Unreadable: Phi-4-mini 12 of 350 (8 bad, 4 clean; mostly provider or connection errors); mimo-v2.6-flash 2 of 350 (1 bad, 1 clean; mostly requests the provider blocked); deepseek-v4-flash 2 of 350 (1 bad, 1 clean; mostly requests the provider blocked).

Dataset v1.1 (2026-11-21): one git diff generator now writes every patch of both classes. In v1.0 the injected part came from another diff tool, and a rule that only looked for a file section without git's `index` line scored J +100%; on v1.1 it scores 0%. Three more format rules were found and removed the same way (table).

All reviewers were run again on v1.1: gpt-6-luna +88% -> +91%, grok-4.1-fast +54% -> +53%, Phi-4-mini -3% -> -4%, deepseek-v4-flash +91% -> +93%, mimo-v2.6-flash +95% -> +98%. No reviewer's J fell by more than its interval when the format tell was removed, so the tell does not explain the first results. The small gains are on the clean side (counting patches with a readable answer in both runs): mimo-v2.6-flash flagged 8 clean patches in the first run and 4 in the second, deepseek-v4-flash flagged 16 clean patches in the first run and 12 in the second, gpt-6-luna flagged 21 clean patches in the first run and 15 in the second, although 174 of the 175 clean patches read the same in both versions apart from the final newline and the length of git's blob ids. Two runs cannot tell run-to-run variation from an effect of that small text change.

Counting hunks is a strong shortcut here: 'two or more hunks in files that already existed' scores J +47% without reading the code, because the injected edit sits in its own hunk, away from the fix. Read the reviewers' J against that baseline, not against 0. (The bare-hunk-header rule is at +6% on v1.1 for the same reason: an injected edit near the top of a file.)

The clean side was tuned after looking at the reviewers' answers. With clean patches matched on file count only (54 + 54), J was +57% for deepseek-v4-flash, +43% for gpt-6-luna and +28% for grok-4.1-fast (mimo +91%). The clean side was then limited to near-minimal patches, a size rule chosen after reading which clean patches the three strong models flagged: +84% / +83% / +58% on 64 + 64 (mimo +94%). The published set uses the filtered clean side.

Hard negatives are left out. A clean patch that also makes a legitimate supporting change in another file cannot appear, because the clean side keeps only near-minimal patches; in a hand check of 12 natural candidates, 6 were such supporting changes and 2 were scope creep. Hard positives (an unrequested edit next to the fix) are left out too: the injected edit is placed in another part of the file or in another file.

The reviewer prompt names the same five kinds of change that the generator was told to inject (refactor, clean-up, extra feature, changed behaviour, added logging or config). A run with a prompt that names no kinds has not been made.

At least 2 of the 175 clean patches hold an unrequested change (one deletes the repository's tox.ini, one rewrites a path in a test fixture): the size filter only blocked new non-Python files. The three strong models flag both.

Injected patches were checked to parse, not run: 36 of the 175 injected edits are quiet behaviour changes, so an injected patch may also be less correct than a clean one. The two sides are not pairs: a clean patch answers another issue and is matched to an injected one on source-file count only.

setup: 151 solutions with the modern API swapped back to its deprecated twin vs 151 untouched solutions, all written by the same 5 models (gpt-6-luna, grok-4.1-fast, Phi-4-mini, deepseek-v4-flash, mimo) for the same tasks, across numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, seaborn, PyTorch, TensorFlow and transformers.

The swap is an automatic code edit (imports, aliases, dotted paths, method and class names), kept only if the result uses the deprecated API and nothing else from the map. Checked against the latest release of each library: 114 of the swapped solutions use a name that is gone, 24 call a function that still exists but raises when called, and 13 still run with a deprecation notice.

Plus 4 hand-written pairs for LLM SDKs (155 + 155 samples in all). Anthropic: a call that names Claude 3.5 Sonnet (retired Oct 28, 2025) and passes temperature (removed from messages.create in SDK 1.x) through a settings object, and a modern streaming call that still names the retired model. Google: a streaming tutor chatbot on the legacy google-generativeai SDK (support ended Nov 30, 2025; imported as `from google import generativeai as genai`) with gemini-pro, and the same chatbot on the current google-genai SDK but still naming gemini-pro. Clean twins use claude-sonnet-5-5 / gemini-3.8-flash on the current SDKs.
Reviewers see the task and the code and are told to assume the latest library versions. Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-20.

The three Claude models (run 2026-11-22) were called through Claude Code in headless mode on a subscription, not through an API: one process per sample with every tool switched off and an empty working folder, the same prompt as the other models plus a one-line system prompt and Claude Code's environment note, default sampling (Claude Code has no temperature setting) and thinking on (it cannot be switched off for these models). No effort level was set: the calls ran at Claude Code's default, which is medium for each of these models (checked 2026-11-22 with the same flags and the same Claude Code version).
caveats: Synthetic: the deprecated calls were swapped in; models writing freely today rarely use these APIs (49 of 956 solutions).

The KG's type checkers were run with the latest version of every library installed (numpy 2.5, pandas 3.1, scipy 1.18, scikit-learn 1.9, PyTorch 2.15, TensorFlow 2.21, transformers 5.23, current Anthropic and Google SDKs): they catch removed APIs (missing attribute or import) and APIs marked @deprecated; mypy finds far fewer because many libraries ship no type information for it. They cannot see a retired model name. The other KG tools tagged obsolescence work before code is written or bump dependency versions. ruff's two rule sets for old APIs cover only NumPy 2 (NPY) and Python-syntax upgrades (UP).
Each zero-shot model was told which failure to look for and was tested on samples that have that failure or none. Its score is a single-prompt, mode-primed estimate, not a product.
Answers with no verdict are left out of the rates; they are not counted as 'not flagged'. Unreadable: deepseek-v4-flash 2 of 310 (1 bad, 1 clean; mostly answers cut by the token budget).

151 of the 155 positives are renames from a deprecation map published in 2024; on those the three strong models catch 99% (gpt-6-luna), 99% (deepseek-v4-flash), 93% (mimo-v2.6-flash). The case that defines this failure, an API retired after the reviewer's knowledge ends, has 4 hand-written pairs: gpt-6-luna caught 1 of 4, deepseek-v4-flash caught 1 of 4, mimo-v2.6-flash caught 1 of 4; grok-4.1-fast flagged all 4 and 4 of the 4 clean twins. Four pairs cannot give a rate; the headline J is about old renames.
A lookup in the 2024 map scores J +97%: it catches all 151 swapped-in calls and none of the 4 SDK retirements. Most of this set measures whether a reviewer knows that map.

The clean side is not fully clean: 5 of the 155 'clean' samples use another deprecated or removed API (3 use TensorFlow 1 names that TensorFlow 2 removed, 2 a deprecated seaborn argument or property). They are 4 of gpt-6-luna's 12 false alarms, 4 of deepseek-v4-flash's 14 false alarms, 4 of mimo-v2.6-flash's 5 false alarms. Malicious names: 82 subtle typos of popular packages (plural, doubled/dropped/swapped letter, keyboard slip, digit, py- prefix; e.g. coloramas, urllib33) and 66 'popular name + word' combosquats (e.g. httpx-utils, twilio-rest).

The three Claude models (run 2026-11-22) were called through Claude Code in headless mode on a subscription, not through an API: one process per sample with every tool switched off and an empty working folder, the same prompt as the other models plus a one-line system prompt and Claude Code's environment note, default sampling (Claude Code has no temperature setting) and thinking on (it cannot be switched off for these models). None of the malicious packages can be installed from PyPI today (all removed). The test is what a reviewer reading the diff can tell.

The name rule is a construction check, not a reviewer. It flags a name that sits near a top-2,000 package and is absent from the 15,000-name download-rank file; the malicious names of this set were chosen as names near a top-2,000 package that are absent from that same file. Its 100% catch rate is built in.

The rule's score is the reach of its allow-list: 82 of 148 genuine names are in the rank file and are cleared without a look. With the list cut to the first 10,000 names its J is +74%, below gpt-6-luna. Of the 15 genuine look-alike or 'name + word' packages outside the file it flags 14; gpt-6-luna flags 1.
By the genuine package of the pair: in the rank file (82 pairs) the rule scores J +99% and gpt-6-luna +73%; outside it (66 pairs) +65% and +82%.

Most model false alarms are an objection to the patch, not a mistake about the name: every patch of this set adds 2-3 dependencies that the fix does not use. setup: 50 pairs. Each starts from one correct agent patch (Qwen3-Coder-480B in OpenHands, hidden tests pass) that uses an existing function. In the positive, that use is replaced by a hand-written re-implementation; the two patches of a pair are identical everywhere else.

What is re-implemented: 30 of the repository's own helpers (e.g. PyJWT's base64url decoding, MONAI's ensure_tuple, oauthlib's raise_from_error, MetPy's check_units decorator), 17 standard-library functions (e.g. shlex.split, fnmatch, os.makedirs(exist_ok=True), csv.writer, functools.wraps, uuid4) and 3 NumPy functions (np.where, np.isclose, np.setdiff1d). How: 33 inline (the call replaced by a few lines), 11 rewritten helpers, 6 copies of the helper's body pasted into the patch.

Each edit was checked: the file still parses, no undefined name is added (ruff F821), the original call is gone and the re-implementation is there. Seven hand-rolled helpers were extracted from the positive patches and run against the function they replace; they agree on the kind of input the patch passes (e.g. shlex.split 6 of 6, fnmatch 36 of 36, fountain's stringify 7 of 8: -0.0 differs). Others differ on edge cases, as hand-rolled code does (time-zone-aware indexes, error classes).

Reviewers see the issue, the patch and, when the re-implemented function is the repository's own, the module that defines it (both patches of a pair see the same files). Same prompt for every model; temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default). Run 2026-11-20. The pairs were written by Claude (the coding assistant building this benchmark), not by any reviewed model.

The three Claude models (run 2026-11-22) were called through Claude Code in headless mode on a subscription, not through an API: one process per sample with every tool switched off and an empty working folder, the same prompt as the other models plus a one-line system prompt and Claude Code's environment note, default sampling (Claude Code has no temperature setting) and thinking on (it cannot be switched off for these models). No effort level was set: the calls ran at Claude Code's default, which is medium for each of these models (checked 2026-11-22 with the same flags and the same Claude Code version).
caveats: Hand-built: every re-implementation was written on purpose. Natural dependency blindness is often larger (whole helpers rebuilt) or subtler.

sentrux, the KG's redundancy checker, was not run: its macOS release binary needs a Gatekeeper quarantine override to start, which was not approved for this run. The rule here is a simple stand-in for its documented duplicate-body check and only catches copied bodies.
Each zero-shot model was told which failure to look for and was tested on samples that have that failure or none. Its score is a single-prompt, mode-primed estimate, not a product.

Answers with no verdict are left out of the rates; they are not counted as 'not flagged'. Unreadable: Phi-4-mini 6 of 100 (3 bad, 3 clean; mostly provider or connection errors). Marked incomplete (under 95% readable in one class): Phi-4-mini.

The three top models are tied on this set: gpt-6-luna +90%, deepseek-v4-flash +86%, mimo-v2.6-flash +86%. gpt-6-luna - deepseek-v4-flash: +4 points, 95% interval -6 to +16; gpt-6-luna - mimo-v2.6-flash: +4 points, 95% interval -6 to +16; deepseek-v4-flash - mimo-v2.6-flash: +0 points, 95% interval -12 to +12 (50 pairs resampled). No best reviewer can be named.

The clean side was selected on the outcome. 8 of 58 drafted pairs were dropped because the strong models flagged their clean side and a re-read found that the agent's own patch already re-implements something. Missed positives and unflagged clean sides were not re-read, so the step removed false alarms of exactly the models that are ranked. Bound: had the 8 clean sides stayed and been flagged, J would be about +77% for gpt-6-luna instead of +90%, and about +72% for deepseek-v4-flash and +72% for mimo.

3 clean sides that two or more models flag are still in the set (db-016, db-020, db-050); the review of 2026-11-21 reads them as the same kind of case as an excluded one, and they were not judged again here. All 50 re-implementations and every decision about what counts as clean were made in one model session (Claude); no second person or model checked them.

For the 30 pairs that re-implement a repository helper the reviewer is shown the module that defines it. In real review, knowing that the helper exists is the hard part. On those pairs gpt-6-luna scores J +90%, deepseek-v4-flash scores J +93%, mimo-v2.6-flash scores J +93%; on the 20 pairs with no file shown +90%, +75%, +75% (same order). A variant with the file left out, or hidden among other files, has not been run.

A rule that compares no code scores J +38%: flag the patch when no function or class of the shown file is named in the added lines (or, with no file shown, when it adds 20 or more lines). The published duplicate-body rule (+12%) finds the 6 pairs that were written as copies, plus both sides of db-051: there the shown file is changed by the patch and is shown as it is after the patch, although the prompt calls it unchanged.

Related measurements exist and are not reproduced here: RepoReuse (Ma et al., arXiv:2609.35357) audits how often coding agents re-implement existing repository code over several turns and reports duplicated logic in 50.8% of task chains by turn 5; DevEval (arXiv:2405.19856) and EvoCodeBench (arXiv:2404.00599) score recall of reference dependencies. This mode asks a different question: does a reviewer notice a re-implementation.
50 pairs: every interval here is about +/-10 points or wider.

findings: On the 2 sets of real agent output (Security vulnerability and False 'done' claims; 2,902 samples) the best reviewer reaches J +23% on Security vulnerability and +46% on False 'done' claims.

Best J: +23% on Security vulnerability and +46% on False 'done' claims; 10 of the 29 ranked rows there have a 95% interval for J that excludes 0. On the 6 sets where the failure was planted on purpose the best reviewer reaches J +83% to +98%; on Logic error (model-written code that is not agent output) +89%. Every set of real agent output scores below every planted set, so this benchmark cannot tell 'reviewers catch these failures' from 'reviewers catch planted failures'. Whether the high scores carry over to failures agents make on their own is not tested.
6 of the 9 sets have constructed positives (Fabrication, Test edits that hide failures, Scope creep, Obsolescence, Supply chain and Dependency blindness).
3 use naturally produced output, 2 of them real agent output. A model-free shortcut baseline is published for 9 of the 9 sets.
A single best reviewer can be named in 2 of 9 modes.

Security vulnerability: claude-opus-5-5 (medium) (J +23%); False 'done' claims: claude-opus-5-5 (medium) (J +46%). In the others the leading rows cannot be told apart at 95% on the samples they share: Fabrication (5 rows, J +93% to +96%); Test edits that hide failures (11 rows, J +86% to +91%); Logic error (2 rows, J +88% to +89%); Scope creep (3 rows, J +96% to +98%); Obsolescence (3 rows, J +94% to +95%); Supply chain (2 rows, J +77% to +83%); Dependency blindness (6 rows, J +78% to +90%).
Where a catalog tool ran its own check (5 of 9 modes), a model asked the failure-specific question was clearly ahead of the best such tool in 4; in 1 no row reaches J 25%.

Ahead: Fabrication (claude-opus-5-5 (medium) +96% vs pyright +85%, difference +10 points on shared samples, 95% interval +6 to +15); Logic error (claude-sonnet-5-5 (medium) +89% vs PR-Agent +53%, difference +35 points on shared samples, 95% interval +30 to +40); False 'done' claims (claude-opus-5-5 (medium) +46% vs PR-Agent +15%, difference +31 points on shared samples, 95% interval +17 to +45); Obsolescence (claude-haiku-5-5 (medium) +95% vs pyright (latest libraries) +57%, difference +38 points on shared samples, 95% interval +24 to +53). No row at J 25%: Security vulnerability. No catalog tool with a check of its own for a finished change was run on Test edits that hide failures, Scope creep, Supply chain and Dependency blindness.
No packaged tool beat the same model asked the failure-specific question (12 comparisons on identical samples: 5 worse, 7 indistinguishable).

Every tool ran with deepseek-v4-flash as its judge model, set by us. Worse: PR-Agent 0.50.0 on Fabrication (-24 points, 95% interval -28 to -19); uqlm 0.6.8 on Logic error (-16 points, 95% interval -23 to -10); PR-Agent 0.50.0 on Logic error (-16 points, 95% interval -20 to -11); Arize Phoenix 3.10.0 on False 'done' claims (-13 points, 95% interval -19 to -6); DeepEval 4.3.4 on False 'done' claims (-19 points, 95% interval -25 to -13). Each of them ran its own general-purpose check, not the failure-specific question. The frameworks that were given our rule text (giskard and promptfoo) were indistinguishable from the bare model in 4 of 4 comparisons.
Free programs reach J 50% or more where the failure is a checkable fact: pyright on Fabrication (+85%); pyright (latest libraries) on Obsolescence (+57%).
No free catalog program within its design scope was run on Test edits that hide failures, Security vulnerability, Logic error, Scope creep, Supply chain and Dependency blindness.
Phi-4-mini scores J under 20% in 6 of the 8 modes it ran in and grok-4.1-fast flags more than 30% of clean samples in 6 of 9 modes.

The other models that ran in at least 8 modes (gpt-6-luna, deepseek-v4-flash, mimo-v2.6-flash, claude-opus-5-5 (medium), claude-sonnet-5-5 (medium) and claude-haiku-5-5 (medium)) score J under 20% in at most 2 modes and flag more than 30% of clean samples in at most 2.
caveats: J compares reviewers within one mode. Do not compare J across modes or average it over them: each set was built differently (real agent runs, model-written functions, injected or hand-built failures) and has its own sample unit, and where the bad samples come from explains most of the difference between modes.

Each zero-shot model was told which failure to look for and was tested on samples that have that failure or none. Its score is a single-prompt, mode-primed estimate, not a product. In use nobody knows which failure a change has, so the prompt of every mode would run on every change and their false alarms add up; the any-flag estimate next to the grid shows by how much. No run with all prompts on the same changes has been made.

Samples are grouped in 6 of 9 modes (Fabrication: 163 files; Security vulnerability: 166 tasks; Logic error: 379 tasks; Obsolescence: 69 API pairs; Supply chain: 148 pairs; Dependency blindness: 50 pairs). Intervals there resample whole groups (100,000 draws). A reviewer is named best only when its paired difference from the runner-up, on the samples both answered, has a 95% interval that excludes 0; otherwise the rows that cannot be told apart are listed as a top group. The best row is still a pick on the test set, so its J is a little optimistic.

Contamination was not assessed. Every set draws on public material (problem sets, GitHub issues and their fixes, CVE fixes, library release notes, package lists), so a model may have seen a task or its answer. Sources: Delulu (Microsoft) (public since 2026-03); Patronus TRACE (public since 2026-01); SusVibes (LeiLiLab) (public since 2025-12); Collu-Bench (lt-asset) (public since 2024-10); SWE-rebench-OpenHands-Trajectories (Nebius) (public since 2025-09); Wang et al. deprecated-API map (ICSE'25) (public since 2024-06); OpenSSF malicious-packages (public since 2023-03). The reviewers' training cut-off dates are not recorded here.

Rates are on answers that carry a verdict. 38 of 143 rows have unreadable answers (the count is beside each row, per label); 10 of them have fewer than 95% readable answers in one class and are marked incomplete.

Same prompt for every model within a mode, temperature 0 (gpt-6-luna: its default), one run each; run-to-run variation was not measured. Prompts and tool settings were fixed before scoring. mypy, ruff and the simple rules are shown in the best of the configurations we ran in each mode, which is a pick on the test set; pyright and mypy on Obsolescence ran with the latest libraries installed.
Baseline rules and shortcut baselines are shown for reference. They are never counted as best and never enter a finding. Rows outside a tool's design scope are listed apart and are not ranked.

A row's cost covers every call made to get its scored answers: the current answer of each sample plus earlier attempts that failed or were cut off and had to be re-run. Smoke tests, runs on earlier versions of a set and accidental duplicate answers are not included. Cost per 1,000 reviews is that cost divided by the reviews made, for one mode-specific question per review. Checking a change for every failure costs the sum over the modes.
The findings above are computed from the rows, so they change with them.

A rule that needs no understanding of the failure reaches J 25% or more on 9 of 9 sets: Fabrication (+60%: context-only rule); Test edits that hide failures (+60%: first user message mentions tests); Security vulnerability (+49%: task prior); Logic error (+39%: surface classifier); False 'done' claims (+61%: issue prior); Scope creep (+47%: two or more hunks in files that already existed); Obsolescence (+97%: the code uses an API listed in the 2024 deprecation map); Supply chain (+100%: an added package is in the OpenSSF malicious-packages list); Dependency blindness (+38%: no name from the shown file appears in the added lines). High reviewer scores on those sets may partly reflect the same shortcut; J 0 is not the right zero there.

star_modes.name: Cascading failure
star_modes.description: The agent detects an error and attempts a fix that introduces NEW errors; repeated iterations spiral further from the working state.
star_modes.note: No dedicated tool yet. The KG's only tag is borderline: agent-governance-toolkit's circuit breakers stop error-rate runaways, not fix-spirals, and it is an experimental template.

tools.name: agent-governance-toolkit
tools.how: Its Agent SRE layer ships a kill switch, SLO/error-budget monitoring and circuit breakers that halt a runaway failing agent loop; aimed at generic error-rate runaways, not fix-spirals specifically.

star_modes.name: Context pollution
star_modes.description: The agent's working context degrades over a session — relevant prior information is dropped, irrelevant material accumulates, or hallucinations from earlier turns are treated as ground truth in later turns.
star_modes.note: No dedicated detector for coding agents yet. The three that detect it are LLM-judge knowledge-retention scores built for chat assistants; several others only work on agents built with them.

tools.name: AutoGen
tools.how: Built-in OpenTelemetry tracing lets a human inspect drift; its buffered/head-tail contexts are token budgeting, not an anti-degradation mechanism.

tools.name: agno
tools.how: Traces runs and tool calls so a human can diagnose drift; no built-in context-pollution check.

tools.name: LangGraph
tools.how: Memory docs name stale or off-topic context as a failure and ship trim/remove/summarize message utilities that the developer must apply; no detection.

tools.name: mlflow
tools.how: Built-in multi-turn KnowledgeRetention LLM judge (experimental) checks whether the assistant retains information from earlier user inputs.

tools.name: mastra
tools.how: Observational Memory compresses old messages into observations so the agent reads what matters instead of stale tool output over long sessions.

tools.name: opik
tools.how: Conversation-thread metrics (Knowledge Retention, Degeneration) check that later replies keep earlier user facts and flag repetition/degeneration.

tools.name: DeepEval
tools.how: Multi-turn LLM-judge metrics (Knowledge Retention, Turn Relevancy) score whether a conversation keeps earlier facts and stays on task.

tools.name: Arize Phoenix
tools.how: OpenTelemetry tracing records the session for human review; no built-in context-degradation metric.

tools.name: TruLens
tools.how: Trace-level Logical Consistency judge flags hallucinations and unsupported assertions, not stale or irrelevant context, so the audit keeps it as records only.
